questions.stem: Customers rate a café’s service as poor, fair, good or excellent. This variable is:
options: categorical ordinal
categorical nominal
numerical discrete
numerical continuous
questions.explanation: The ratings are categories with a natural order, which makes them ordinal. Nominal categories, such as hair colour, have no order at all.

questions.stem: Which of the following variables is numerical and discrete?
options: The time taken to run 100 metres
The suburb a student lives in
A shirt size recorded as S, M or L
The number of cars owned by a household
questions.explanation: A count of cars can only take whole-number values, so it is discrete numerical data. A running time is measured on a continuous scale, and suburb and shirt size are categorical.

questions.stem: The five-number summary of a data set consists of:
options: the mean, median, mode, range and IQR
the minimum, mean, median, mode and maximum
Q1, median, Q3, the IQR and the range
the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum
questions.explanation: The five-number summary is the minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum, which are the values a boxplot is drawn from. The mean and mode are not part of it.

questions.stem: On a boxplot, a data value is shown as a possible outlier if it is less than:
options: the median − 1.5 × IQR
Q1 − 1.5 × the range
Q1 − 1.5 × IQR
Q1 − IQR
questions.explanation: The lower fence is Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and the upper fence is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. The fences are measured from the quartiles, not from the median.

questions.stem: For a bell-shaped distribution, the 68–95–99.7% rule says that about 95% of the values lie:
options: above two standard deviations below the mean
within three standard deviations of the mean
within two standard deviations of the mean
within one standard deviation of the mean
questions.explanation: About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. Above two standard deviations below the mean is 97.5% of values, not 95%.

questions.stem: A standardised score (z-score) is calculated as:
options: (data value − mean) × standard deviation
data value ÷ standard deviation
(data value − mean) ÷ standard deviation
(mean − data value) ÷ standard deviation
questions.explanation: A z-score counts how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, so subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. Subtracting the other way round reverses the sign, putting values above the mean below zero.

questions.stem: When a scatterplot is drawn, the explanatory variable is placed on:
options: the horizontal axis
the vertical axis
whichever axis has the larger values
the axis with the smaller range
questions.explanation: By convention the explanatory variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis and the response variable on the vertical (y) axis. The scale of the values does not decide the axis.

questions.stem: Pearson’s correlation coefficient, r, measures:
options: the slope of the least squares line
the strength and direction of a linear association
the strength of any association, linear or not
the percentage of variation that is explained
questions.explanation: r describes only linear association, from −1 to 1, and its sign gives the direction. The percentage of variation explained is given by r², the coefficient of determination.

questions.stem: On a logarithmic (base 10) scale, the value 4 represents:
options: 10⁴⁰
questions.explanation: A log value of 4 means 10⁴, which is 10 000. Each step of 1 on a base 10 log scale multiplies the original value by 10, so 3 represents 1000.

questions.stem: A histogram has most of its values at the low end and a long tail stretching to the right. The distribution is:
options: positively skewed
negatively skewed
symmetric
bimodal
questions.explanation: Skew is named after the tail, and a tail to the right (towards larger values) is positive skew. A negatively skewed distribution has its tail to the left.

questions.stem: A back-to-back stem plot is suitable for showing the association between:
options: two categorical variables with two categories each
a numerical variable and a categorical variable with many categories
a numerical variable and a categorical variable with two categories
two numerical variables measured on the same subjects
questions.explanation: Each side of a back-to-back stem plot shows the numerical values for one of two groups. Two numerical variables need a scatterplot, and a categorical variable with more than two categories needs parallel boxplots or dot plots.

questions.stem: Cause and effect between two variables can only be firmly established by:
options: a large observational study
a high coefficient of determination
a controlled experiment
a strong correlation coefficient
questions.explanation: An experiment controls the other variables, so a change in the response can be put down to the explanatory variable. Even a very strong correlation from observed data can be explained by other variables.

questions.stem: Nine values are: 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 20. The interquartile range is:
questions.explanation: The median is 9, so Q1 is the median of 3, 5, 6, 8, which is 5.5, and Q3 is the median of 11, 12, 14, 20, which is 13. IQR = 13 − 5.5 = 7.5; 17 is the range.

questions.stem: A data set has Q1 = 12 and Q3 = 20. Which of these values would be shown as an outlier on a boxplot?
questions.explanation: IQR = 8, so the fences are 12 − 12 = 0 and 20 + 12 = 32. Only 33 lies beyond a fence; 0 sits exactly on the lower fence, and a value must be below the fence to be an outlier.

questions.stem: Adult male heights are approximately normally distributed with mean 176 cm and standard deviation 7 cm. The percentage taller than 190 cm is about:
questions.explanation: 190 cm is two standard deviations above the mean, and 95% of heights lie within two standard deviations, so 5% lie outside and half of that, 2.5%, is above. 5% counts both tails.

questions.stem: A test has mean 65 and standard deviation 8. A student who scored 53 has a standardised score of:
questions.explanation: z = (53 − 65) ÷ 8 = −12 ÷ 8 = −1.5. The negative sign shows the score is below the mean; −12 is the difference before dividing by the standard deviation.

questions.stem: Mia scored 72 in English (mean 64, standard deviation 4) and 80 in Maths (mean 71, standard deviation 6). Relative to her classmates, she did:
options: better in Maths, with z = 1.5 compared with 1.33
better in Maths, because 80 is the higher score
equally well, because both scores are above the mean
better in English, with z = 2 compared with 1.5
questions.explanation: English: z = (72 − 64) ÷ 4 = 2. Maths: z = (80 − 71) ÷ 6 = 1.5. The higher z-score shows the better relative performance, even though the raw Maths score is higher.

questions.stem: Packets of rice have weights that are approximately normal with mean 1000 g and standard deviation 5 g. A packet with a standardised score of −2 weighs:
questions.explanation: The weight is the mean plus z standard deviations: 1000 + (−2 × 5) = 990 g. Using +2 instead gives 1010 g, which is above the mean.

questions.stem: The values 3, 5, 6, 8 and 13 have a mean of 7. Correct to two decimal places, their sample standard deviation is:
questions.explanation: The squared deviations sum to 16 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 36 = 58. Dividing by n − 1 = 4 gives 14.5, and √14.5 ≈ 3.81. Dividing by n gives √11.6 ≈ 3.41, 14.50 is the variance before the square root, and 2.80 is the mean absolute deviation.

questions.stem: The body masses of mammals range from a few grams to thousands of kilograms, so a log (base 10) scale is used. A log mass of 2.5 corresponds to a mass of about:
questions.explanation: A log value of 2.5 means 10 to the power 2.5, which is 10² × √10 ≈ 100 × 3.16 ≈ 316 g. Multiplying 2.5 by 100 to get 250 treats the log scale as if it were linear.

questions.stem: A town has a population of 50 000. On a log (base 10) scale, this population is plotted at about:
questions.explanation: 50 000 = 5 × 10⁴, and log 5 ≈ 0.7, so log 50 000 ≈ 4.7. Counting the zeros gives 4, which ignores the factor of 5; 3.7 is the log of 5000.

questions.stem: A log (base 10) scale is most useful for displaying a variable when the data:
options: are all clustered close to the mean
have been recorded as categories
range over several orders of magnitude
contain a few negative values
questions.explanation: A log scale turns each multiplication by 10 into one equal step, so very small and very large values can be shown on one axis. The log of a negative number or zero is undefined, so negative values cannot be plotted.

questions.stem: Of 80 dog owners surveyed, 20 exercise daily. Of 120 people without a dog, 18 exercise daily. The percentage of people without a dog who exercise daily is:
questions.explanation: The percentage is taken within the group: 18 ÷ 120 = 0.15, or 15%. Dividing by all 200 people surveyed gives 9%, and 47% is 18 out of the 38 people who exercise daily.

questions.stem: A survey asks whether the age group of an adult (under 40, 40 and over) is associated with their main news source. To compare the groups, percentages should be calculated:
options: within each age group, the explanatory variable
within each news source, the response variable
as a share of everyone in the whole survey
within the largest group, then applied to the rest
questions.explanation: Age group is the explanatory variable, so the percentages are found within each age group and then compared across the news sources. Calculating them within news source answers a different question.

questions.stem: In a survey, 60% of adults under 40 used online news as their main source, compared with 35% of adults aged 40 and over. This suggests that:
options: online news is used by 95% of adults surveyed
news source is associated with age group
age group is not associated with news source
being under 40 causes people to read news online
questions.explanation: The percentage using online news differs clearly between the age groups, so the variables are associated. The survey is observational, so it cannot show that age causes the choice, and the percentages come from different groups so cannot be added.

questions.stem: A study investigates whether the hours of sunshine in a day can be used to predict ice-cream sales. The explanatory variable is:
options: the ice-cream sales
the day of the week
the price of an ice-cream
the hours of sunshine
questions.explanation: The explanatory variable is the one used to explain or predict the other, so it is the hours of sunshine. Ice-cream sales respond to the sunshine, making them the response variable.

questions.stem: A researcher asks whether resting pulse rate is associated with whether a person smokes. The explanatory variable and its type are:
options: pulse rate, a categorical variable
smoking status, a categorical variable
pulse rate, a numerical variable
smoking status, a numerical variable
questions.explanation: Smoking status is thought to explain differences in pulse rate, and its values (smoker, non-smoker) are categories. Pulse rate is the numerical response variable.

questions.stem: Parallel boxplots show weekly study hours for students with and without a part-time job. The median is 12 hours for those with a job and 18 hours for those without; the IQRs are similar. This suggests that:
options: having a part-time job causes students to study six fewer hours
job status is associated with study hours only if the ranges differ
study hours are associated with job status, as the median is lower for students with a job
study hours are not associated with job status, as the IQRs are similar
questions.explanation: A clear difference in median between the groups is evidence of an association between the variables. Similar IQRs only tell us the spreads match, and an observational comparison cannot prove cause.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows a linear association with r = −0.62. The association is best described as:
options: moderate, positive and linear
moderate, negative and linear
weak, negative and linear
strong, negative and linear
questions.explanation: Using the usual guidelines, 0.5 ≤ |r| < 0.75 is moderate, and the negative sign shows the response tends to fall as the explanatory variable rises. Strong requires |r| of 0.75 or more.

questions.stem: A scatterplot shows a clear U-shaped pattern, yet r = 0.05. The best conclusion is that:
options: there is no association of any kind between the two variables
there is a weak positive linear association between the variables
the value of r must have been calculated incorrectly
there is a clear non-linear association but almost no linear association
questions.explanation: r only measures linear association, and a U shape has rising and falling parts that cancel out, so r is close to zero. The plot itself shows a clear non-linear pattern.

questions.stem: For a strongly skewed distribution with an outlier, the most suitable summary statistics for centre and spread are:
options: the mean and the standard deviation
the mean and the IQR
the median and the range
the median and the IQR
questions.explanation: The median and IQR are based on the middle of the data, so they are not pulled by the tail or the outlier. The mean, standard deviation and range are all affected by extreme values.

questions.stem: A stem plot (key: 2|3 = 23) has rows 1 | 5 8, 2 | 0 3 3 7, 3 | 1 4 and 4 | 9. The median is:
questions.explanation: The nine values in order are 15, 18, 20, 23, 23, 27, 31, 34, 49, and the fifth is 23. Choosing 27 takes the middle of the 20s row rather than the middle of the whole data set.

questions.stem: Two classes sat the same test. Class A had mean 70 and standard deviation 4; Class B had mean 70 and standard deviation 12. Which statement is correct?
options: The classes had the same centre and the same spread of scores.
Class A’s scores were more spread out, because 4 is closer to 0.
The classes had the same centre, but Class B’s scores were more spread out.
Class B performed better, because its standard deviation is larger.
questions.explanation: Equal means show the same centre, and the larger standard deviation shows Class B’s scores varied more about that centre. The standard deviation says nothing about which class did better.

questions.stem: In a survey of Year 12 students, those who slept more hours had higher average marks. A teacher concludes that more sleep causes higher marks. This conclusion is not justified because:
options: marks would have to be the explanatory variable in this study
the data are observational, so other variables could explain the association
the association between sleep and marks must be negative
sleep is a categorical variable and marks are numerical
questions.explanation: In an observational study the researcher does not control other variables, such as study habits or health, which could affect both sleep and marks. Only an experiment can establish cause and effect.

questions.stem: Weights of lambs are approximately normal with mean 60 kg and standard deviation 5 kg. The percentage of lambs weighing between 55 kg and 70 kg is about:
questions.explanation: 55 kg is one standard deviation below the mean (34%) and 70 kg is two above (47.5%), giving 34% + 47.5% = 81.5%. 68% covers only one standard deviation either side.

questions.stem: Packet weights are approximately normal with mean 500 g and standard deviation 4 g. In a batch of 2000 packets, the number expected to weigh more than 504 g is about:
questions.explanation: 504 g is one standard deviation above the mean. 68% lie within one standard deviation, so 32% lie outside and 16% lie above; 16% of 2000 is 320. 640 counts both tails.

questions.stem: A five-number summary is 4, 18, 24, 30, 52. When the boxplot is drawn:
options: only the minimum, 4, is shown as an outlier
both the minimum and the maximum are outliers
neither the minimum nor the maximum is an outlier
only the maximum, 52, is shown as an outlier
questions.explanation: IQR = 30 − 18 = 12, so the fences are 18 − 18 = 0 and 30 + 18 = 48. The maximum 52 is above 48, but the minimum 4 is above the lower fence of 0.

questions.stem: For five pairs of values, the sum of the products of the standardised scores, z(x) × z(y), is 3.2. The correlation coefficient r is:
questions.explanation: r = Σ z(x) z(y) ÷ (n − 1) = 3.2 ÷ 4 = 0.8. Dividing by n = 5 gives 0.64, and r can never exceed 1, so 3.2 is impossible.

questions.stem: Among primary school children, shoe size and reading ability have r = 0.85. The most likely explanation for this association is that:
options: the association is caused by the larger sample
both variables increase with age, a common response
larger feet help children to read more fluently
reading more causes children’s feet to grow
questions.explanation: Older children have both larger feet and better reading skills, so age drives both variables. Neither variable causes the other, which is why a strong correlation alone cannot establish cause.

questions.stem: Children’s heights are recorded in centimetres and r = 0.72 with their weights. If the heights are converted to metres, the value of r becomes:
questions.explanation: r is calculated from standardised scores, which do not change when every value is multiplied by the same positive number. A change of units therefore leaves r unchanged.

questions.stem: Sixty tomato plants are randomly allocated to receive a new fertiliser or no fertiliser, and the fertilised plants produce more fruit. A causal conclusion can be drawn because:
options: random allocation balances other factors across the two groups
sixty plants is a large enough sample to show any effect
fruit yield is a numerical variable that can be measured
the fertilised plants produced a larger mean fruit yield
questions.explanation: This is an experiment: random allocation means differences in soil, light and so on are spread evenly between the groups, so the fertiliser is the only systematic difference. A difference in means alone, without that control, would not show cause.

questions.stem: Ice-cream sales and the number of drownings at Victorian beaches are strongly positively associated. The best non-causal explanation is:
options: a coincidence of two random series
drownings leading to more sales
a common response to hot weather
ice-cream causing swimmers to tire
questions.explanation: Hot weather increases both ice-cream sales and the number of people swimming, so both variables respond to a third variable. Coincidence is unlikely when an obvious common cause explains the pattern.

questions.stem: Two numerical variables have r = 0.30. A student claims that, because r is positive, there is a strong positive association. The student is wrong because:
options: a positive r shows only the slope, not the direction
r must be above 0.95 for any association to exist
r = 0.30 indicates a weak positive linear association
r = 0.30 indicates a moderate negative association
questions.explanation: The sign of r gives the direction, but its size gives the strength, and 0.25 ≤ |r| < 0.5 is described as weak. Any value of r other than about 0 can indicate some linear association.

questions.stem: A data set has a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 6. One value has a z-score of 2.5. This value is:
questions.explanation: Data value = mean + z × standard deviation = 40 + 2.5 × 6 = 55. Adding 6 alone, to get 46, treats the value as just one standard deviation above the mean.

questions.stem: A two-way table shows 45 of 150 city residents and 30 of 60 country residents own a ute. Comparing ute ownership by location, the percentages are:
options: city 60%, country 40%
city 45%, country 30%
city 21%, country 14%
city 30%, country 50%
questions.explanation: Within each location: 45 ÷ 150 = 30% and 30 ÷ 60 = 50%. The split 60% and 40% comes from dividing the 75 ute owners between locations, which answers a different question.
